draft.title: The doctrine of precedent
card: A decision of a higher court in the same court hierarchy must be followed by lower courts in later cases with similar facts. For example, a Victorian County Court must follow the Victorian Court of Appeal.
Other decisions need not be followed but a court may consider them. These include decisions of lower courts, courts in other hierarchies and courts overseas.
A higher court can reverse a decision on appeal in the same case. It can overrule an earlier precedent in a different case, so that the old rule no longer stands.

A court can distinguish a precedent if the facts of the new case are materially different, and so not follow it. A court can disapprove of a decision, which expresses doubt without changing the result.
draft.remember: Higher courts bind lower courts in the same hierarchy, and the rest only persuade.

a.q: A Magistrates' Court in Victoria hears a case with facts like an earlier Victorian Court of Appeal decision. What must the Magistrates' Court do?
opts: Follow the Court of Appeal decision, which is binding
Consider the decision, but it is only persuasive
Overrule the Court of Appeal decision
Wait for parliament to pass a new Act
a.why: The Court of Appeal is higher in the same hierarchy, so its decision binds the Magistrates' Court. It is not merely persuasive, and a lower court cannot overrule a higher one.
a.clue: Think about which court is higher in the same hierarchy.

b.q: A County Court judge in Victoria finds that the facts before her differ in an important way from a binding precedent. She decides not to follow it. What has she done?
b.why: Distinguishing means finding a material difference in the facts, so the precedent does not apply. Overruling is done by a higher court in a later case. Reversing happens on appeal in the same case.
b.clue: Her reason was the facts, not a view that the old rule was wrong.

a.best: Follow the Court of Appeal decision, which is binding
